blocks.text: A man with metastatic melanoma, expected to live only months, is given an antibody that does not attack the tumour at all. It simply removes a brake on his own T cells. Years later the tumour deposits are gone. The same drug can cause severe colitis, because the brake was also protecting his gut.

blocks.markdown: **Immune surveillance** is the idea that the immune system recognises and eliminates transformed cells before they form tumours. Tumour cells carry **neoantigens** (peptides from mutated proteins) and abnormally expressed self proteins, which can be presented on MHC class I to **CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells**; **NK cells** also kill cells that have lost MHC class I. Evidence includes the higher incidence of some cancers (virus-related tumours, skin cancers) in immunosuppressed patients. Tumours that arise despite this have by definition **evaded** the immune response.

rows: Loss or downregulation of MHC class I, or defects in antigen processing (e.g. TAP)
CD8⁺ T cells cannot see the tumour (but NK cells may detect the missing self)
Cells lacking the targeted antigen are selected for
Tumour and stromal cells secrete TGF-β and IL-10; recruitment of regulatory T cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells
Tumour cells do not express CD80/CD86, so T cells become anergic
Tumour cells express PD-L1, engaging PD-1 on T cells and switching them off (T cell exhaustion)
blocks.caption: How tumours evade immune surveillance

blocks.markdown:
**Immune checkpoints** are inhibitory receptors that normally restrain T cell responses and protect against autoimmunity. Two are therapeutically important:

- **CTLA-4** is expressed on activated T cells and on Tregs. It binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells with higher affinity than CD28, outcompeting co-stimulation and damping T cell **priming**, mostly in lymph nodes.
- **PD-1** is expressed on activated and exhausted T cells. It binds **PD-L1** (and PD-L2) on tumour cells and other tissues, recruiting phosphatase (SHP2) that dampens TCR and CD28 signalling and thereby inhibits T cell **effector function** in the tumour and peripheral tissues.

blocks.title: Checkpoint inhibitor
blocks.text: A monoclonal antibody that blocks an inhibitory receptor or its ligand (CTLA-4, PD-1 or PD-L1), releasing the brake on T cells and allowing an existing anti-tumour response to proceed.

blocks.title: Matching the brake to the drug
blocks.prompt: Explain how an anti-PD-1 antibody and an anti-CTLA-4 antibody differ in where and how they act, and why the two can be combined.

steps.text: Anti-CTLA-4 (e.g. ipilimumab) blocks CTLA-4 so CD28 can bind CD80/86; this enhances priming and expansion of T cells in lymph nodes and reduces Treg-mediated restraint.
Anti-PD-1 (e.g. pembrolizumab, nivolumab) or anti-PD-L1 (e.g. atezolizumab) blocks the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction, restoring effector function of exhausted T cells inside the tumour.
The sites and stages differ (priming versus effector phase), so the effects are complementary and the combination can be more active.
The cost is more immune-related adverse events, because the same brakes protect normal tissues.

blocks.answer: CTLA-4 blockade boosts priming; PD-1 blockade restores effector function; the combination is complementary but more toxic.

blocks.markdown: **Immune-related adverse events.** Releasing T cell checkpoints causes autoimmune-like inflammation: colitis and diarrhoea, dermatitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, and endocrinopathies such as thyroiditis and hypophysitis. They often respond to corticosteroids and sometimes require stopping the drug. Tumours with many mutations (high neoantigen load) tend to respond better, and PD-L1 expression is sometimes used as a biomarker.

**CAR T cell therapy.** A **chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)** is a synthetic receptor. Its extracellular part is a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) taken from an antibody, so it recognises a surface antigen **without MHC restriction**; its intracellular part joins the T cell signalling domain **CD3ζ** to a **co-stimulatory domain** (CD28 or 4-1BB), so the engineered cell gets signals 1 and 2 in one step. The process is:

1. Collect the patient's T cells by leukapheresis.
2. Introduce the CAR gene with a viral vector (retroviral or lentiviral).
3. Expand the cells in culture.
4. Give the patient lymphodepleting chemotherapy, then infuse the CAR T cells.

CAR T cells directed against **CD19** are used in relapsed B cell leukaemia and lymphoma. CD19 is also on normal B cells, so **B cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia** are expected on-target effects. Other toxicities are **cytokine release syndrome** (fever and hypotension from massive IL-6 and other cytokine release, treated with the IL-6 receptor antibody tocilizumab) and **neurotoxicity**.

rows: The patient's own T cells, by blocking CTLA-4 or PD-1/PD-L1
T cells engineered to carry a CAR
A well-defined surface target antigen (e.g. CD19)
Cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, B cell aplasia
blocks.caption: Comparing two immunotherapy strategies

blocks.title: Estimating a cell dose
blocks.prompt: (Illustrative arithmetic.) A CAR T product is prescribed at 2 × 10^6 CAR T cells per kg body mass. How many cells does a 70 kg patient receive, and what fraction of a tumour burden of 10^10 cells is that number?

steps.text: Multiply dose per kg by mass.

Interpretation: the infused cells are a small fraction of the tumour cell number, but they proliferate in vivo after antigen encounter and each can kill many targets, so expansion is essential to the effect.

blocks.answer: 1.4 × 10^8 cells; about 1.4% of the tumour cell number.

blocks.title: Tumour escape and therapy are mirror images
blocks.text: Tumours evade by hiding from T cells (lost MHC I, lost antigen), suppressing them (TGF-β, Tregs, PD-L1) or starving them of co-stimulation. Checkpoint inhibitors undo suppression; CAR T cells bypass MHC loss by recognising surface antigen directly.

points: Tumours evade immune surveillance by losing MHC class I or antigens, creating an immunosuppressive environment, lacking co-stimulation and expressing PD-L1.
Anti-CTLA-4 enhances T cell priming and anti-PD-1/PD-L1 restores effector function; both can cause immune-related adverse events.

CAR T cells are engineered T cells carrying an scFv-CD3ζ-costimulatory receptor that recognises surface antigen without MHC; toxicities include cytokine release syndrome and B cell aplasia (for CD19).

questions.stem: Which change would help a tumour escape CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells?

options.text: Increased expression of MHC class I
Loss of TAP or MHC class I expression

questions.correctOptionText: Loss of TAP or MHC class I expression

distractorRationale.a: More MHC class I would improve recognition.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: without peptide-MHC I, CD8⁺ T cells cannot recognise the tumour.

questions.explanation: CD8⁺ T cells recognise peptide on MHC class I. Tumours that lose MHC I or antigen processing escape this recognition, though NK cells may detect the missing self.

questions.stem: A tumour secretes TGF-β and IL-10 and recruits regulatory T cells. How does this aid immune evasion?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these factors suppress effector T cell function.
distractorRationale.b: They do not increase MHC class I expression.
distractorRationale.c: They do not enhance NK killing.

questions.explanation: TGF-β, IL-10 and Tregs suppress effector T cells in the tumour microenvironment, allowing the tumour to grow despite neoantigens.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the mechanism of pembrolizumab?

options.text: It blocks PD-1 on T cells, preventing PD-L1 from inhibiting them
It binds CD19 on tumour cells to deplete B cells
It activates CD28 on B cells

questions.correctOptionText: It blocks PD-1 on T cells, preventing PD-L1 from inhibiting them

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is an anti-PD-1 antibody that restores T cell effector function.
distractorRationale.b: That describes anti-CD19 or CAR T cell targeting.
distractorRationale.c: Anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab block TNF.

questions.explanation: Pembrolizumab is an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor. By preventing PD-1 engagement with PD-L1, it releases exhausted T cells in the tumour.

questions.stem: Why does anti-CTLA-4 therapy increase T cell priming?

options.text: CTLA-4 normally outcompetes CD28 for CD80/86, so blocking it allows greater co-stimulation

questions.correctOptionText: CTLA-4 normally outcompetes CD28 for CD80/86, so blocking it allows greater co-stimulation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CTLA-4 has higher affinity for B7 than CD28.
distractorRationale.c: It does not block MHC class I.
distractorRationale.d: It does not deplete B cells.

questions.explanation: CTLA-4 binds CD80/86 with higher affinity than CD28 and delivers inhibitory signals; blocking it increases co-stimulation and T cell activation in lymph nodes.

questions.stem: A patient receiving a checkpoint inhibitor develops severe diarrhoea and colitis two months into therapy. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: An immune-related adverse event from loss of checkpoint-mediated tolerance
Cytokine release syndrome from CAR T cells

questions.correctOptionText: An immune-related adverse event from loss of checkpoint-mediated tolerance

distractorRationale.a: Correct: checkpoint blockade can cause autoimmune-like colitis.
distractorRationale.b: The patient is not receiving CAR T cells.
distractorRationale.d: Complement deficiency does not explain this.

questions.explanation: Checkpoints maintain tolerance in tissues, so blocking them can trigger autoimmune-like inflammation such as colitis, dermatitis or thyroiditis.

questions.stem: True or false: a CAR T cell recognises its target antigen only when it is presented on the patient's MHC molecules.
questions.explanation: A CAR uses an antibody-derived scFv to recognise a surface antigen directly, without MHC restriction. This allows CAR T cells to work even when tumours have lost MHC class I.

questions.stem: A CAR T product is prescribed at 1 × 10^6 cells/kg. Calculate the total number of cells, in units of 10^7, for a patient weighing 85 kg.
questions.explanation: Total cells = 1 × 10^6 × 85 = 8.5 × 10^7. This is a teaching calculation of weight-based dosing; actual dosing follows product labelling.

questions.stem: A tumour burden of 2 × 10^9 cells is reduced to 4 × 10^7 cells by treatment. What percentage of tumour cells has been eliminated?
questions.explanation: Fraction remaining = 4 × 10^7 / 2 × 10^9 = 0.02. Eliminated = 1 - 0.02 = 0.98, or 98%. Even this high kill leaves 4 × 10^7 cells, which is why sustained immune control is needed.

questions.stem: Describe four mechanisms by which tumours evade immune surveillance.
markingGuide: Downregulation of MHC class I or antigen processing defects
Immunosuppressive cytokines (TGF-β, IL-10), Tregs and myeloid-derived suppressor cells
PD-L1 expression causing T cell exhaustion
questions.explanation: Tumours avoid recognition (MHC, antigen) or suppress the response (cytokines, Tregs, PD-L1, absent co-stimulation).

questions.stem: Explain how PD-1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibitors work, and outline the principle of CAR T cell therapy, including one toxicity of each.
markingGuide: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7; blockade increases T cell priming
PD-1 binds PD-L1 and inhibits effector function; blockade restores killing
Toxicity of checkpoint inhibitors: immune-related adverse events (colitis, thyroiditis, hepatitis)
CAR T: patient T cells collected, engineered with scFv-CD3ζ-costimulatory receptor, expanded, infused after lymphodepletion
Recognises surface antigen independent of MHC (e.g. CD19); toxicity: cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity or B cell aplasia
questions.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors release the brakes on existing T cells, while CAR T cells provide a new engineered specificity.
